adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:274 — result.errors.email` is truthy for ANY email error (already taken, domain not allowed, transient), so the client permanently caches that email as `user.email.invalid`, disables submit, and hides the real reason for the rest of the session.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a client-side `rejectedEmails` cache. On account creation failure, it unconditionally does `pushObject(result.values.email)` whenever `result.errors.email` is present (create_account_controller.js ~274). `emailValidation` then checks `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` and returns `failed: true` with the generic `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`, regardless of the actual server-side error (taken, not_allowed, blocked, etc.), and the computed property is wired to `rejectedEmails.@each`. This will cause the same email to be treated as permanently invalid for the remainder of the controller lifecycle and mask the real reason on subsequent validations.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:17 — rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` is defined on the class prototype (shared by all instances) and is never cleared, so rejections leak across modal open/close and controller instances.

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` is a mutable array created at definition time inside `Discourse.CreateAccountController = Discourse.Controller.extend(...)`. In Ember, such objects are placed on the prototype/defaults and can be shared/persist across the controller’s lifetime rather than being re-initialized per modal open. The diff also only ever `pushObject`s into it (on failed create) and never clears it, so previously rejected emails can continue to be treated as invalid on subsequent uses without a server re-check.

app/models/blocked_email.rb:16 — record.save` return value is ignored (a failed save silently drops stats) and it runs the BlockedEmail uniqueness validation, adding an extra SELECT+UPDATE per matching unauthenticated POST /users — cheap write amplification for an attacker hammering a blocked address.

adjudication.rationale: In BlockedEmail.should_block? the code unconditionally mutates and calls `record.save` (line shown in diff) to update `match_count`/`last_match_at`, and the return value isn’t checked. If the save fails (validation/DB issue), the method will still return based on `record.action_type`, silently dropping the stats update. Also, because `save` runs validations including `validates :email, uniqueness: true`, each blocked signup attempt can incur extra DB work (and always an UPDATE) creating write amplification on unauthenticated `/users` requests.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13 — record.errors[attribute].blank?` short-circuits `should_block?` whenever presence/uniqueness/domain-list errors already exist, so a blocked email that is also domain-blacklisted or already registered never updates `match_count`/`last_match_at` (inconsistent tracking).

adjudication.rationale: In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, the blocked-email check is gated by `if record.errors[attribute].blank? and BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`. Since `User` now runs presence/uniqueness validations before this validator (`validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true`), and domain whitelist/blacklist errors are also added earlier in this same method, any pre-existing `:email` error will prevent calling `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, so `match_count`/`last_match_at` won’t be updated in those cases. This is a real behavioral implication of the diff, but it only affects tracking/metrics (the signup would already fail), so it’s not clearly a correctness bug unless full tracking was intended.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/user.rb:47 — if: :email_changed?` means an existing account whose email is later added to `blocked_emails` is never re-validated on save; blocking is signup-only and the `:do_nothing` tracking never sees existing users, which is undocumented.

adjudication.rationale: In `app/models/user.rb` the new validator is `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`, and `EmailValidator` is where `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` (and the whitelist/blacklist logic) runs. That means blocked-email checks (and the match_count/last_match_at tracking side effects in `BlockedEmail.should_block?`) only execute when a user's `email` attribute is dirty—i.e., on signup/new record and on email-change updates, but not on arbitrary saves of existing users if the blocked list changes later. This is a real scope/behavior implication created by the diff, but it’s not clearly a defect since retroactively invalidating existing accounts is not shown as a requirement in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — Read-modify-write of match_count (`+= 1` then save) is not atomic; concurrent signups lose increments (use increment_counter/update_all).

adjudication.rationale: In app/models/blocked_email.rb#should_block?, it loads a record then does `record.match_count += 1` followed by `record.save`. This is a classic non-atomic read-modify-write; concurrent calls can overwrite each other and lose increments to match_count (and potentially last_match_at), since there’s no locking or atomic UPDATE (e.g., update_all/increment_counter).

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:274 — Any errors.email (including uniqueness "has already been taken" and presence) pushes the email into rejectedEmails and the field is then labelled user.email.invalid and submit disabled, misreporting duplicate-account emails as invalid.

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, on any failed create where `result.errors.email` is present, it unconditionally pushes `result.values.email` into `rejectedEmails` (lines ~271-276). Then `emailValidation` short-circuits and returns `{ failed: true, reason: I18n.t('user.email.invalid') }` whenever the current email is in `rejectedEmails` (new block around line ~65). Since `users_controller#create` now returns `errors: user.errors.to_hash`, uniqueness/presence/blocked/etc. email errors will all set `errors.email`, so a "has already been taken" uniqueness error will be treated as permanently "invalid" in the field validation rather than reflecting the actual error.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb:5 — action_type is NOT NULL with no DB default while the only default lives in a before_validation callback, so any insert that bypasses validations (raw SQL/COPY "manually load the table" per spec comment, save(validate: false), insert) fails with a not-null violation.

adjudication.rationale: The migration creates `blocked_emails.action_type` as `null: false` with no DB-level default (db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb:5-8). The only default is set in `BlockedEmail` via `before_validation :set_defaults` (`self.action_type ||= ...`), which only runs through ActiveRecord validations. Any insert path that bypasses validations (raw SQL/COPY/manual loading, `save(validate: false)`, etc.) and omits `action_type` will hit a NOT NULL violation. This is especially relevant given the spec comment about “manually load the table with some emails,” which would commonly omit `action_type`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb:10 — Unique index on email is case-sensitive (no lower(email)) and signup email is never downcased (User.new_from_params assigns params[:email] raw; Email.downcase only used in change_email), so blocked rows can be duplicated by case and case-variant signups silently bypass the block.

adjudication.rationale: The new blocked email mechanism is case-sensitive end-to-end: the migration adds a unique index on `blocked_emails.email` with no functional lowercasing, `BlockedEmail` validates `uniqueness: true` (case-sensitive by default), and `BlockedEmail.should_block?` does an exact `where(email: email)` lookup. In `EmailValidator`, it passes the raw `value` into `should_block?` without normalizing case. As a result, a blocked entry like `bad@spam.com` would not match a signup using `Bad@Spam.com`, and duplicate blocked rows differing only by case are possible despite the “unique” constraint.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 — should_block? does an exact-match where(email:) with no normalization (strip/downcase), so "Block@SpamFromHome.org" does not match a stored "block@spamfromhome.org" row.

adjudication.rationale: In app/models/blocked_email.rb, `should_block?(email)` performs `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`, which is an exact string match and the method does not normalize (`strip`/`downcase`) the input email. Since emails are commonly treated case-insensitively, a user-provided value like `Block@SpamFromHome.org` would not match a stored `block@spamfromhome.org` row, potentially bypassing the new blocking logic added via `EmailValidator` (`BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`).

matched_golden_ids: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both point to the same underlying problem: the email-block “check” triggers a DB write to update stats (match_count), creating side effects during what should be a read/validation and introducing concurrency/race issues (lost updates due to non-atomic read-modify-write). The candidate doesn’t mention the misleading method name, but it captures the core side-effect + race-condition concern.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:8 — action_type stores positional Enum ints (Enum.new(:block, :do_nothing)); inserting or reordering members later silently remaps existing rows, with no explicit value mapping or comment guarding the order.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `BlockedEmail.actions` as `Enum.new(:block, :do_nothing)` and persists the selected value in the `blocked_emails.action_type` integer column (migration adds `t.integer :action_type, null: false`). This implies positional integer mapping based on declaration order; if members are later inserted/reordered, existing rows could be reinterpreted without any explicit mapping or comment guarding order. That’s a real, diff-grounded maintainability/data-compat risk, but not an immediate functional bug shown by this PR alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 — should_block? does an exact case-sensitive `where(email:)` lookup while User.new_from_params (user.rb:87) stores params[:email] raw with no downcase/strip, so `Bad@Spam.com`, ` bad@spam.com` or `bad+x@spam.com` trivially bypass a block on `bad@spam.com`.

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, `BlockedEmail.should_block?(email)` does an exact `where(email: email)` lookup with no normalization (no `strip`/`downcase`) and `BlockedEmail` stores `email` as a plain string. The new `EmailValidator` passes the raw `value` into `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` with no normalization either. This means the blocking behavior is sensitive to the exact string provided, so variants like different casing or leading/trailing whitespace can evade a blocked entry depending on how emails are stored/compared.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:20 — Domain restriction regexp `@(domains)` is unanchored, so whitelist `example.com` also accepts `user@example.com.evil.net` / `user@example.company`, defeating the whitelist (pre-existing, moved into this new "comprehensive" validator; setting is admin-controlled and only dots are escaped).
matched_golden_ids: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both describe the same underlying flaw: the domain whitelist regex `@(#{domains})` is not properly anchored/boundaried, so matching can occur on domain suffix/prefix substrings, allowing bypasses (e.g., extra labels like `example.com.evil.net` or similar). This is the same issue as allowing attacker-controlled domains to pass a whitelist for `example.com`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:13 — Unauthenticated signup attempts perform a DB write (match_count++, last_match_at, full save) on every match; with no rate limiting in users#create beyond the static honeypot, an attacker can spam the endpoint to corrupt the admin-facing block statistics and add write load per request.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, which performs a DB write (`match_count += 1`, `last_match_at = ...`, `record.save`) on every validation attempt that matches a `blocked_emails` row. This method is invoked from the new `EmailValidator` during `User` email validation (`validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`), which will run on unauthenticated signup (`UsersController#create`). That creates a write-amplification / stats-poisoning surface for blocked emails. The finding’s additional claim about “no rate limiting beyond honeypot” is not verifiable from this diff alone, but the write-on-unauthenticated-validation behavior is diff-grounded.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/users_controller.rb:197 — New field-level `errors` hash plus distinct "is not allowed." vs "not allowed from that email provider" vs "has already been taken" messages give an unauthenticated oracle for whether a given address is on the BlockedEmail list or already registered (the taken/domain cases already leaked via `message`; the blocklist case is new).

adjudication.rationale: The diff makes the unauthenticated `UsersController#create` failure response include structured `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and adds a new distinct validation message for blocked emails (`user.email.blocked: "is not allowed."` via `EmailValidator` + `BlockedEmail.should_block?`). This enables a client (or attacker) to distinguish cases like blocked vs domain-not-allowed vs uniqueness (“has already been taken”) by inspecting `errors[:email]` (and also via the returned `message` composed from `full_messages`). That’s a security information disclosure/oracle introduced by this change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb:9 — Validator spec only covers the BlockedEmail branch and never exercises the whitelist/blacklist branches moved from User#email_validator or the errors[attribute].blank? gating that skips the block check.

adjudication.rationale: The new `EmailValidator#validate_each` includes both the domain whitelist/blacklist logic and a gated blocked-email check (`if record.errors[attribute].blank? and BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`). The added spec `spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb` only stubs/exercises `BlockedEmail.should_block?` true/false and does not cover the whitelist/blacklist branches or verify that an existing error on `:email` prevents calling/blocking via `BlockedEmail.should_block?`. This is a concrete, diff-grounded test coverage gap for newly centralized logic, not a runtime defect by itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb:11 — Both validator tests stub BlockedEmail.should_block?, so no test creates a real BlockedEmail record and asserts a User with that email fails validation/save end-to-end.

adjudication.rationale: In spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb both examples stub BlockedEmail.should_block? (returns false/true) and only assert on record.errors[:email] after calling validate_each directly. No test exercises the real BlockedEmail.should_block? implementation (which queries/updates blocked_emails) or an end-to-end User validation/save failing when a matching BlockedEmail record exists. Given the diff adds nontrivial DB-backed logic in lib/validators/email_validator.rb and app/models/blocked_email.rb, this is a concrete missing-coverage concern rather than a functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/users_controller.rb:198 — New errors/values keys in the users#create failure JSON (consumed by the JS rejectedEmails logic) have no controller spec asserting their presence or shape.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new JSON keys on user creation failure in `UsersController#create` (`errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice(...)`), and the frontend change (`rejectedEmails` in `create_account_controller.js`) conditionally relies on `result.errors.email` and `result.values.email`. The diff introduces specs for `EmailValidator` and `BlockedEmail`, but does not add any controller/request spec asserting the presence/shape of these new response fields, so the finding is diff-grounded and specific (API contract lacks test coverage), but not itself a functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 — No test covers case/whitespace variants (e.g. Block@SpamFromHome.org) even though should_block? does an exact-match where(email:) and User has no email-downcasing hook before validation, so the block is trivially bypassable and untested.

adjudication.rationale: The new blocking logic in `BlockedEmail.should_block?(email)` does an exact match lookup (`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`) with no normalization (no downcasing/stripping shown in `User` validations or `EmailValidator`). That makes the newly introduced email-block feature trivially bypassable via case/whitespace variants (e.g., `Block@SpamFromHome.org`), and the added specs only cover exact-match behavior, not normalization/variants.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:69 — No JS test for rejectedEmails: neither the pushObject on result.errors.email nor emailValidation failing for a previously rejected email.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new client-side state and validation logic (`rejectedEmails: Em.A([])`, a new early-return failure in `emailValidation` when `rejectedEmails.contains(email)`, and pushing into `rejectedEmails` on failed create when `result.errors.email` is present). No corresponding JS test changes are included in the diff (only Ruby model/validator specs are added), so the newly added client-side behavior is untested in this PR.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb:19 — Assertion only checks errors[:email] is present, not that the message is user.email.blocked, so adding the not_allowed message from the wrong branch would still pass.

adjudication.rationale: In spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb, the “adds an error when email matches a blocked email” example only asserts `record.errors[:email].should be_present` after stubbing `BlockedEmail.should_block?` to return true. Since EmailValidator first can add `user.email.not_allowed` based on `SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist/blacklist` before adding `user.email.blocked`, this test would still pass even if the validator added the wrong error message or never added the `blocked` message (as long as some email error is present). This is a test precision gap, not a functional defect proven by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb:23 — should_block? returns nil (record && ...) rather than false when no record exists; be_false passes on nil under RSpec 2 but the spec does not pin the documented false contract.

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, when no record exists `record` is `nil` and the method returns `record && record.action_type == actions[:block]`, i.e. `nil` rather than a literal `false`. This isn’t a functional defect for current usage (it’s used in a boolean context in `EmailValidator`), but it does contradict the implied boolean contract and the spec wording (“returns false…”). Tightening the method to return a boolean (or tightening the spec to assert `nil` vs `false`) would make the contract explicit.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb:12 — "last_match_at is null" is trivially true for any freshly created record and verifies no behavior of the model.

adjudication.rationale: The spec `it "last_match_at is null" do ... BlockedEmail.create(email: email).last_match_at.should be_nil` will indeed always pass given the diff: `BlockedEmail#set_defaults` only sets `action_type` and neither the model nor the migration assigns a default for `last_match_at`, so it remains `NULL` by default. While arguably a low-value/tautological test, it still reflects the current behavior (nothing sets `last_match_at` on create) and is essentially a test-quality nit rather than a concrete diff-grounded defect or significant review issue.
